sets.title: A rack for a guitar
sets.transcript:

M: Sure, it's quick and cheap. But a guitar's too wide for a rack. It'd hit your legs. Most people just wear the case on their back.
W: Oh, OK. I'll try that first.

sets.title: Dad's old drum kit
sets.transcript:
M: Hey, come and look what I found behind the boxes in the garage. Dad's old drum kit.
W: Wow, I forgot we still had that. He hasn't played it since before I was born.
M: Exactly. It's just taking up space. I looked online, and a kit like this sells for about three hundred dollars. That's a hundred and fifty each.
W: We can't sell it. It's Dad's, not ours. And I think he'd be sad. Mom says he played in a band in college.
M: But he never even talks about it. I bet he wouldn't notice it was gone.
W: Maybe not. But I'd like to keep it. I could learn to play.
M: You? You gave up the piano after three months.
W: That was different. I hated the teacher. Anyway, we could set it up in the corner of the garage.
M: There's no room. Dad needs that space for the car in winter. And drums are really loud. The neighbors would complain.
W: Hmm, you're right about the noise. Mrs. Penrow next door already complains about our dog. She'd hate drums.
M: So what do we do with it? It can't stay behind those boxes forever. Look, the drum skins are starting to crack.
W: Wait, what about your school? Didn't your music teacher say they need more instruments for the after-school band?
M: Mr. Nadler? Yeah, he did. They've only got one old drum, and the kids take turns on it.
W: So we could lend it to the school. It stays Dad's, it gets played, and it's out of the garage.
M: Lend it, not give it away. I like that. But we still have to ask Dad first.
W: Of course. He's at the hardware store until four. When he gets back, I'll show him the kit and ask him. You write to Mr. Nadler tonight and see if the school even wants it.
M: Deal. And if Dad says no, well, at least we tried.

sets.title: Saving a painted cave
sets.transcript:
OK, so last week we looked at how people painted animals on cave walls thousands of years ago. Today I want to talk about a problem those paintings face in our own time, and about one solution that was tried.

Picture this. In nineteen forty, a few teenagers exploring the hills in France found a narrow opening in the ground. They climbed down, and the walls inside were covered with paintings of horses, deer and huge wild cattle, in reds, yellows and blacks. The paintings were roughly seventeen thousand years old, and they were in amazing condition. Why? Because for all that time, the cave had been sealed. The air inside barely moved. The temperature stayed almost the same, all year round.

A few years later, the cave was opened to visitors, and it became hugely popular. By the nineteen fifties, more than a thousand people a day were walking through it. Now, here's the problem. Every visitor breathes out warm, wet air. Bring in a thousand people a day, and the air in a small cave changes completely. It gets warmer, and the walls get damp. Visitors also carried in tiny living things on their shoes and clothes. Before long, green patches of algae, which are simple plant-like growths, started spreading across the rock. The very people who'd come to admire the paintings were slowly harming them.

So what was the solution? In nineteen sixty-three, the cave was closed to the public. Completely. About twenty years later, a copy was opened nearby. Artists spent years recreating the most famous walls with the same kinds of colors, so visitors could see something close to the real thing without breathing on it.

Did it work? This is where it gets complicated. Closing the cave stopped the crowds, and the algae was brought under control. But around the year two thousand, a white fungus suddenly spread across the floor and walls, decades after the visitors had gone. Then black spots appeared. Scientists still argue about why. Some point to a new air-control system that had just been put in. Others blame the chemicals used to kill the fungus, which may have fed the next outbreak. Honestly, nobody's sure, and every treatment seems to change the cave in a new way.

The copy raises its own question, too. And I have to say, the copy is better than I expected. I've seen photos of a real wall and the copied wall side by side, and I couldn't tell them apart, not even the colors. Still, there's an argument that the point of a place like that is standing where the painters actually stood, and no copy can give you that. The other argument is that if the choice is between a copy and losing the paintings forever, the copy wins easily.

So I can't give you a neat ending today. Closing the cave clearly helped with the first problem. Whether it's enough to save the paintings in the long run, we just don't know yet. For next class, write half a page on this question. If a painted cave were found near here tomorrow, would you open it to visitors or not, and why?
